sections.title: What Is Quantization?
sections.body: > **Quantization is the process of reducing the numerical precision of a model's weights and activations — from high-precision floating point numbers (32-bit or 16-bit) down to lower-precision formats (8-bit, 4-bit, or even 2-bit) — so the model uses dramatically less memory and runs dramatically faster, with minimal loss in quality.**

sections.title: The Core Concept — Numbers Take Space
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              THE FUNDAMENTAL PROBLEM                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  A NEURAL NETWORK IS JUST NUMBERS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LLaMA-3 8B  = 8,000,000,000 parameters (weights)
  Each weight = one number

  The question is: HOW PRECISELY do we store each number?

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PRECISION OPTIONS:                                      │
  │                                                          │
  │  FP32  (32-bit float):  1.23456789012345...              │
  │        Range: ±3.4 × 10^38                               │
  │        Size:  4 bytes per number                         │
  │                                                          │
  │  FP16  (16-bit float):  1.2345...                        │
  │        Range: ±65,504                                    │
  │        Size:  2 bytes per number                         │
  │                                                          │
  │  BF16  (bfloat16):      1.234...                         │
  │        Range: ±3.4 × 10^38  (same range as FP32!)        │
  │        Size:  2 bytes per number                         │
  │                                                          │
  │  INT8  (8-bit int):     123  (integers only)             │
  │        Range: -128 to 127                                │
  │        Size:  1 byte per number                          │
  │                                                          │
  │  INT4  (4-bit int):     12   (integers only)             │
  │        Range: -8 to 7                                    │
  │        Size:  0.5 bytes per number                       │
  │                                                          │
  │  INT2  (2-bit int):     1                                │
  │        Range: -2 to 1                                    │
  │        Size:  0.25 bytes per number                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LLAMA-3 8B MODEL SIZE AT DIFFERENT PRECISIONS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  8B parameters × bytes per parameter:

  FP32:   8B × 4 bytes  =  32 GB  ← needs A100 GPU ($10K+)
  FP16:   8B × 2 bytes  =  16 GB  ← needs RTX 3090/4090
  BF16:   8B × 2 bytes  =  16 GB  ← same as FP16
  INT8:   8B × 1 byte   =   8 GB  ← fits RTX 3080 10GB!
  INT4:   8B × 0.5 bytes=   4 GB  ← fits RTX 3060 8GB!
  INT2:   8B × 0.25bytes=   2 GB  ← fits on laptop GPU!!

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  32 GB → 4 GB  =  8x memory reduction                   │
  │  Same model. Similar quality. Fraction of the cost.     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

sections.title: Types of Quantization
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              QUANTIZATION TAXONOMY                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  DIMENSION 1: WHEN does quantization happen?
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  POST-TRAINING QUANTIZATION (PTQ):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Train model in FP32/BF16                               │
  │       ↓                                                  │
  │  AFTER training: compress weights to INT8/INT4           │
  │       ↓                                                  │
  │  Run inference with quantized model                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ✅ Simple — no retraining needed
  ✅ Works on any pre-trained model (LLaMA, Mistral, etc.)
  ✅ Minutes to quantize
  ❌ Small quality loss (can't recover precision)

  QUANTIZATION-AWARE TRAINING (QAT):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Train/fine-tune model                                  │
  │  SIMULATE quantization DURING training                   │
  │       ↓                                                  │
  │  Model LEARNS to be accurate at lower precision          │
  │       ↓                                                  │
  │  Quantize after training                                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ✅ Better quality than PTQ
  ✅ Model adapts to quantization
  ❌ Requires training (expensive)
  ❌ More complex setup

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  DIMENSION 2: WHAT gets quantized?
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  WEIGHT-ONLY QUANTIZATION:
  Only compress the stored weights.
  Activations (intermediate values) stay in FP16.

  Weights:      INT4  (stored compressed)
  Activations:  FP16  (computed at runtime)
  Computation:  Dequantize weights → FP16 → compute

  ✅ Maximum memory savings
  ✅ Simple implementation
  ❌ Still needs FP16 compute (GPU requirements same)

  WEIGHT + ACTIVATION QUANTIZATION:
  Compress both weights AND activations.

  Weights:      INT8
  Activations:  INT8
  Computation:  INT8 × INT8 = INT16/INT32

  ✅ Fastest inference (INT8 math is faster than FP16)
  ✅ Memory savings for both storage and compute
  ❌ Harder to implement correctly
  ❌ Activations have dynamic range (harder to quantize)

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  DIMENSION 3: HOW are weights grouped?
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  PER-TENSOR: One scale for ALL weights in entire model
  PER-LAYER:  One scale per layer
  PER-CHANNEL:One scale per output channel (row of weight matrix)
  PER-GROUP:  One scale per GROUP of N weights (e.g., 128 weights)

  More granular = better quality = more overhead
  Per-group (group_size=128) is the sweet spot for INT4.
```

sections.title: Major Quantization Methods Explained
sections.body:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              THE 6 MAJOR QUANTIZATION METHODS                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  METHOD 1: GPTQ (Generative Pre-trained Transformer Quantization)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Year: 2022 | Type: PTQ | Best for: 4-bit, 8-bit

  KEY IDEA: Use a calibration dataset to find the BEST quantized
  weights — not just the nearest integer, but the integers that
  minimize the error in the layer's OUTPUT.

  Algorithm (simplified):
  1. Feed calibration data through the model
  2. For each layer:
     a. Quantize one weight column at a time
     b. Measure the error this introduces
     c. Compensate remaining weights to minimize error
     d. This is "optimal brain compression" (OBC)
  3. Result: quantized weights that are better than naive rounding

  NAIVE QUANTIZATION:    weight 1.234 → nearest INT4 = 1
  GPTQ:                  weight 1.234 → best INT4 = 1 (but then
                         adjust other weights to compensate for
                         accumulated error in this row)

  Quality: ★★★★☆  Speed to quantize: ★★★☆☆  (needs calibration data)

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  METHOD 2: GGUF / llama.cpp (Q4_K_M, Q8_0, etc.)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Year: 2023 | Type: PTQ | Best for: CPU inference, consumer HW

  KEY IDEA: Format optimized for llama.cpp — runs models on CPU
  (and GPU via Metal/CUDA). Includes quantization in the file format.

  GGUF quantization types:
  ┌────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Format    │  Description                                  │
  ├────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Q4_0      │  4-bit, basic. Fastest, lowest quality.      │
  │  Q4_K_S    │  4-bit, K-quant small. Better than Q4_0.     │
  │  Q4_K_M    │  4-bit, K-quant medium. ← BEST BALANCE       │
  │  Q5_K_M    │  5-bit, K-quant. Higher quality.             │
  │  Q6_K      │  6-bit. Near-FP16 quality.                   │
  │  Q8_0      │  8-bit. Best quality, 2x FP16 size.          │
  │  F16       │  Full FP16. No quantization.                 │
  └────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  "K-quant" = keeps important weights at higher precision,
              quantizes less important weights more aggressively.

  Quality: ★★★★☆  CPU speed: ★★★★★  GPU speed: ★★★☆☆

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  METHOD 3: AWQ (Activation-Aware Weight Quantization)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Year: 2023 | Type: PTQ | Best for: 4-bit with best quality

  KEY IDEA: Not all weights are equally important.
  Some weights correspond to HIGH-ACTIVATION channels
  (they process features the model cares about most).
  Protect those important weights → keep at higher precision.

  The insight:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  0.1% of weights are "salient" (high activation scale)  │
  │  These 0.1% cause 80% of quantization error if squished │
  │                                                          │
  │  AWQ finds these important weights                       │
  │  Scales them UP before quantization                      │
  │  (amplify → quantize → scale back down at inference)     │
  │  Result: important weights get effectively more bits     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Quality: ★★★★★  Speed: ★★★★☆  Memory: ★★★★☆
  → BEST quality 4-bit method for production inference

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  METHOD 4: bitsandbytes (BnB) — LLM.int8() and QLoRA's NF4
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Year: 2022-2023 | Type: PTQ | Best for: training + inference

  TWO KEY INNOVATIONS:
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  A) LLM.int8() — 8-bit inference:
  Discovers that weight matrices have a few "outlier" columns
  with very large values. Quantizing those columns to INT8
  causes major quality loss.

  Solution:
  - Find outlier feature dimensions (say 0.1% of columns)
  - Keep those in FP16
  - Quantize remaining 99.9% to INT8
  - Mixed-precision matrix multiplication at runtime

  B) NF4 (Normal Float 4-bit) — used in QLoRA:
  LLM weights follow a NORMAL DISTRIBUTION (bell curve).
  Regular INT4 has evenly spaced values: -8,-7,-6,-5...,7
  NF4 has values CLUSTERED around 0 (where most weights live!):
  More values near center → less error for typical weights

  NF4 values: -1.0, -0.69, -0.52, -0.39, -0.28, -0.18,
               -0.10, -0.04, 0, 0.04, 0.10, 0.18, 0.28,
               0.39, 0.52, 0.69, 1.0
  (normalized to [-1, 1], densely spaced near 0)

  Quality: ★★★★☆  Training compatibility: ★★★★★

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  METHOD 5: GGML / Q4_K_M explained in detail
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  "K-quant" strategy: different layers quantized differently!

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Attention layers:  more important → Q6_K (6-bit)       │
  │  FFN layers:        less important → Q4_K (4-bit)       │
  │  Embeddings:        critical       → Q8_0 (8-bit)       │
  │  Output layer:      critical       → Q8_0 (8-bit)       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Mixed precision within ONE model = best quality/size ratio

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  METHOD 6: EXL2 (ExLlamaV2 format)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Year: 2023 | Type: PTQ | Best for: GPU, mixed-precision

  KEY IDEA: Per-layer mixed quantization with calibration.
  Measure each layer's sensitivity → allocate bits accordingly.
  Average 4 bits but some layers get 3, some get 5.

  EXL2 2.5bpw  = average 2.5 bits per weight (very small)
  EXL2 4.0bpw  = average 4 bits (standard)
  EXL2 6.0bpw  = average 6 bits (high quality)

  Quality: ★★★★★  GPU speed: ★★★★★  Flexibility: ★★★★★
```

sections.body:
```python name=quantization/method1_bitsandbytes.py
"""
METHOD 1: BitsAndBytes Quantization
INT8 (LLM.int8()) and INT4 (NF4 for QLoRA)
Most widely used for HuggingFace models.
"""
import torch
from transformers import (
    AutoTokenizer,
    AutoModelForCausalLM,
    BitsAndBytesConfig,
)

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# OPTION A: INT8 Quantization (LLM.int8())
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def load_int8_model(model_name: str):
    """
    Load model in INT8 using bitsandbytes LLM.int8().

    How it works:
    - Identifies outlier feature dimensions
    - Keeps outlier columns in FP16
    - Quantizes rest to INT8
    - Mixed-precision matmul at inference

    Memory: ~50% of FP16 baseline
    Quality: ~97% of FP16
    """
    print(f"\n  Loading {model_name} in INT8...")

    bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
        load_in_8bit              = True,
        llm_int8_threshold        = 6.0,   # Outlier threshold
        llm_int8_has_fp16_weight  = False,
        llm_int8_skip_modules     = None,  # Modules to keep in FP16
    )

    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    model     = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        model_name,
        quantization_config = bnb_config,
        device_map          = "auto",      # Auto GPU placement
        torch_dtype         = torch.float16,
    )

    # Check memory usage
    mem_gb = sum(
        p.element_size() * p.nelement()
        for p in model.parameters()
    ) / 1e9
    print(f"  ✅ INT8 model loaded: {mem_gb:.2f} GB")
    return model, tokenizer

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# OPTION B: INT4 / NF4 Quantization (for QLoRA)
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def load_nf4_model(model_name: str):
    """
    Load model in 4-bit NF4 quantization.
    This is the config used in QLoRA fine-tuning!

    NF4 = Normal Float 4-bit
    - Values clustered around 0 (matches weight distribution)
    - Double quantization: quantize the quantization scales too!
    - compute_dtype=BF16: fast BF16 math during forward pass

    Memory: ~25% of FP16 baseline
    Quality: ~91% of FP16
    """
    print(f"\n  Loading {model_name} in NF4 (4-bit)...")

    bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
        load_in_4bit              = True,
        bnb_4bit_quant_type       = "nf4",       # Normal Float 4
        bnb_4bit_compute_dtype    = torch.bfloat16,  # Fast compute
        bnb_4bit_use_double_quant = True,        # Quantize scales too!
        bnb_4bit_quant_storage    = torch.uint8, # Storage dtype
    )

    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    model     = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        model_name,
        quantization_config = bnb_config,
        device_map          = "auto",
        trust_remote_code   = True,
    )

    mem_gb = sum(
        p.element_size() * p.nelement()
        for p in model.parameters()
    ) / 1e9
    print(f"  ✅ NF4 model loaded: {mem_gb:.2f} GB")
    return model, tokenizer

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# DOUBLE QUANTIZATION EXPLAINED IN CODE
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def explain_double_quantization():
    """
    Double Quantization = quantize the quantization constants.

    Regular NF4:
    - Each group of 64 weights has 1 scale factor (FP32 = 4 bytes)
    - 8B params / 64 = 125M groups
    - Scale overhead = 125M × 4 bytes = 500 MB extra!

    Double Quantization:
    - Quantize those scale factors too (to 8-bit)
    - Scale overhead = 125M × 1 byte = 125 MB
    - Saves 375 MB ← meaningful for large models!
    """
    print("""
    Without Double Quantization:
    Weights:    4-bit NF4
    Scales:     FP32 (one per 64 weights) → large overhead

    With Double Quantization:
    Weights:    4-bit NF4
    Scales:     8-bit (quantized!) → smaller overhead
    Scale-scales: FP32 (tiny) → minimal overhead

    Net saving: ~0.37 bits per weight → extra ~3.6 GB saved
                for a 70B model!
    """)

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# INFERENCE WITH QUANTIZED MODEL
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def run_inference(model, tokenizer, prompt: str) -> str:
    """
    Run inference on any quantized model.
    Same code works for INT8, NF4, GPTQ, AWQ.
    """
    inputs = tokenizer(
        prompt,
        return_tensors = "pt",
    ).to(model.device)

    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model.generate(
            **inputs,
            max_new_tokens  = 200,
            do_sample       = True,
            temperature     = 0.7,
            top_p           = 0.9,
            pad_token_id    = tokenizer.eos_token_id,
        )

    # Decode only the new tokens
    new_tokens = outputs[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]
    return tokenizer.decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True)

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# COMPARE: FP16 vs INT8 vs NF4 quality
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def compare_quantization_quality(model_name: str):
    """
    Load same model in different precisions and compare outputs.
    Shows quality vs size tradeoff in practice.
    """
    prompt = "Explain the concept of attention in transformers:"

    results = {}

    # Load NF4 (smallest)
    model_nf4, tok_nf4 = load_nf4_model(model_name)
    results["NF4 (4-bit)"] = run_inference(model_nf4, tok_nf4, prompt)
    del model_nf4
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()

    # Load INT8
    model_int8, tok_int8 = load_int8_model(model_name)
    results["INT8 (8-bit)"] = run_inference(model_int8, tok_int8, prompt)
    del model_int8
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()

    print(f"\n  📊 Quality Comparison for: '{prompt[:40]}'")
    print(f"  {'─'*55}")
    for method, output in results.items():
        print(f"\n  [{method}]:")
        print(f"  {output[:200]}...")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Replace with any HuggingFace model
    MODEL = "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct"

    print("=" * 60)
    print("BITSANDBYTES QUANTIZATION DEMO")
    print("=" * 60)

    explain_double_quantization()

    # INT8 example
    model, tokenizer = load_int8_model(MODEL)
    response = run_inference(
        model, tokenizer,
        "What is quantization in machine learning?"
    )
    print(f"\nINT8 Response: {response[:200]}")
```

```python name=quantization/method2_gptq.py
"""
METHOD 2: GPTQ Quantization
Post-training quantization with calibration data.
Uses auto-gptq or optimum library.
"""
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# OPTION A: Quantize a model yourself with GPTQ
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def quantize_with_gptq(
    model_name:     str,
    output_dir:     str,
    bits:           int  = 4,
    group_size:     int  = 128,
    n_calibration:  int  = 128,
):
    """
    Quantize a model to GPTQ format.

    Steps:
    1. Load calibration dataset (small set of real text)
    2. Run model on calibration data → measure activations
    3. For each layer: find optimal quantized weights
       that minimize layer output error
    4. Save quantized model

    Args:
        bits:          Number of bits (2, 3, 4, 8)
        group_size:    Weights per quantization group (64, 128)
        n_calibration: Number of calibration samples
    """
    from transformers import AutoTokenizer
    from auto_gptq import AutoGPTQForCausalLM, BaseQuantizeConfig

    print(f"\n  Quantizing {model_name} to {bits}-bit GPTQ...")
    print(f"  Group size: {group_size} | Calibration: {n_calibration}")

    # ── Step 1: Prepare calibration data ──────────────
    print("  Loading calibration dataset...")
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)

    # Use wikitext for calibration (standard practice)
    dataset = load_dataset("wikitext", "wikitext-2-raw-v1",
                           split="train")
    texts = [
        t for t in dataset["text"]
        if len(t) > 100
    ][:n_calibration]

    # Tokenize calibration samples
    calibration_data = []
    for text in texts:
        tokens = tokenizer(
            text,
            return_tensors  = "pt",
            max_length      = 512,
            truncation      = True,
            padding         = False,
        )
        calibration_data.append(tokens["input_ids"])

    # ── Step 2: Configure GPTQ ─────────────────────────
    quantize_config = BaseQuantizeConfig(
        bits            = bits,
        group_size      = group_size,
        damp_percent    = 0.01,     # Damping for numerical stability
        desc_act        = True,     # Descending activation order
                                    # (better quality for 4-bit)
        static_groups   = False,
        sym             = False,    # Asymmetric quantization
        true_sequential = True,     # Layer-by-layer (more accurate)
        model_name_or_path = model_name,
        model_file_base_name = "model",
    )

    # ── Step 3: Load and quantize ──────────────────────
    print("  Loading model for quantization...")
    model = AutoGPTQForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        model_name,
        quantize_config = quantize_config,
        low_cpu_mem_usage = True,
        torch_dtype     = torch.float16,
    )

    print("  Running GPTQ quantization (this takes a while)...")
    model.quantize(calibration_data)

    # ── Step 4: Save quantized model ──────────────────
    print(f"  Saving quantized model to {output_dir}...")
    model.save_quantized(
        output_dir,
        use_safetensors = True,     # More secure format
    )
    tokenizer.save_pretrained(output_dir)

    print(f"  ✅ GPTQ quantization complete!")
    print(f"  Bits: {bits} | Group size: {group_size}")
    return output_dir

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# OPTION B: Load pre-quantized GPTQ model (easier!)
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def load_gptq_model(model_name: str):
    """
    Load a pre-quantized GPTQ model from HuggingFace.
    Many models are pre-quantized: TheBloke/*, etc.

    Example model names (TheBloke provides many):
    "TheBloke/LLaMA-2-7B-GPTQ"
    "TheBloke/Mistral-7B-v0.1-GPTQ"
    "TheBloke/CodeLlama-13B-GPTQ"
    """
    from transformers import AutoTokenizer
    from auto_gptq import AutoGPTQForCausalLM

    print(f"\n  Loading GPTQ model: {model_name}")

    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
        model_name, use_fast=True
    )

    model = AutoGPTQForCausalLM.from_quantized(
        model_name,
        use_safetensors  = True,
        trust_remote_code= False,
        device_map       = "auto",
        use_triton       = False,       # True = faster but needs triton
        quantize_config  = None,
    )

    # Model memory
    mem_gb = sum(
        p.element_size() * p.nelement()
        for p in model.parameters()
    ) / 1e9
    print(f"  ✅ GPTQ model loaded: {mem_gb:.2f} GB GPU memory")
    return model, tokenizer

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# GPTQ ALGORITHM VISUALIZATION
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def visualize_gptq_algorithm():
    """Show how GPTQ works conceptually."""
    print("""
    GPTQ ALGORITHM — HOW IT WORKS:

    For each layer weight matrix W (shape: [out, in]):
    ════════════════════════════════════════════════

    Step 1: Compute Hessian H from calibration data
            H = 2XX^T  where X = layer inputs from calibration
            H tells us: "which weights matter most?"

    Step 2: For each weight column j (in order of importance):
            ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
            │  q_j = quantize(w_j)                         │
            │  (snap weight to nearest quantization level)  │
            │                                               │
            │  error = w_j - q_j  ← quantization error    │
            │                                               │
            │  Update remaining weights:                    │
            │  W[:, j+1:] -= error × H^{-1}[j, j+1:]      │
            │           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^    │
            │           This COMPENSATES for the error     │
            │           in this column by adjusting the    │
            │           remaining columns!                  │
            └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    Step 3: Result: quantized weights that minimize
            the layer's OUTPUT error, not just weight error.

    WHY THIS IS BETTER THAN NAIVE ROUNDING:
    Naive:  just round each weight independently
            Error accumulates → significant quality loss

    GPTQ:   each rounding error is compensated
            in subsequent weights
            Much lower final output error ✅
    """)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    visualize_gptq_algorithm()

    # To quantize a model yourself:
```

```python name=quantization/method3_awq.py
"""
METHOD 3: AWQ — Activation-Aware Weight Quantization
Best quality 4-bit quantization. Used in production.
"""
import torch

def visualize_awq_insight():
    """Show AWQ's core insight with a concrete example."""
    print("""
    AWQ's KEY INSIGHT:
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

    OBSERVATION: In transformer layers, activations are NOT
    uniformly distributed. Some input channels consistently
    have MUCH higher activation magnitudes.

    Example layer activations (per channel):
    Channel 0:  avg activation = 0.12  ← small
    Channel 1:  avg activation = 0.08  ← small
    Channel 2:  avg activation = 0.11  ← small
    Channel 3:  avg activation = 8.74  ← LARGE! (salient)
    Channel 4:  avg activation = 0.09  ← small
    Channel 5:  avg activation = 0.13  ← small
    Channel 6:  avg activation = 7.21  ← LARGE! (salient)
    ...

    Only ~1% of channels are salient but they cause ~80% of
    quantization error when naively quantized to INT4!

    AWQ SOLUTION:
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

    For salient channel j with scale factor s_j:

    BEFORE AWQ:
    y = Wx   (normal matrix multiply)
    Q(W)x   = quantize W naively → big error on salient channels

    AWQ TRICK:
    y = W × x
      = (W × diag(s)) × (diag(s)^{-1} × x)
      = W' × x'

    Where:
    W' = W × diag(s)  ← scale UP the salient weights before quant
    x' = diag(s)^{-1} × x  ← scale DOWN the activations to match

    Effect on quantization:
    Original weight w = 0.02 (salient channel)
    Scale s = 4.0
    Scaled weight w' = 0.08
    Quantized w' → INT4: better resolution for this weight!

    At inference:
    Scale activations by 1/s before multiply → mathematically identical
    But quantized weights have MUCH less error ✅

    RESULT:
    ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    AWQ 4-bit ≈ GPTQ 4-bit quality
    AWQ is FASTER to quantize (no long calibration)
    AWQ is better at preserving important channel information
    """)

def load_awq_model(model_name: str):
    """
    Load AWQ quantized model.

    Pre-quantized models available on HuggingFace:
    "TheBloke/LLaMA-2-7B-AWQ"
    "TheBloke/Mistral-7B-v0.1-AWQ"
    "TheBloke/CodeLlama-13B-AWQ"
    "casperhansen/llama-3-8b-instruct-awq"
    """
    from awq import AutoAWQForCausalLM
    from transformers import AutoTokenizer

    print(f"\n  Loading AWQ model: {model_name}")

    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    model     = AutoAWQForCausalLM.from_quantized(
        model_name,
        fuse_layers     = True,    # Kernel fusion for speed
        trust_remote_code=False,
        safetensors     = True,
    )

    print(f"  ✅ AWQ model loaded")
    return model, tokenizer

def quantize_with_awq(
    model_name:    str,
    output_dir:    str,
    w_bit:         int = 4,
    q_group_size:  int = 128,
    zero_point:    bool= True,
):
    """
    Quantize a model with AWQ.
    Much faster than GPTQ — no iterative optimization.
    """
    from awq import AutoAWQForCausalLM
    from transformers import AutoTokenizer

    print(f"\n  AWQ quantizing {model_name} to {w_bit}-bit...")

    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    model     = AutoAWQForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        model_name,
        low_cpu_mem_usage=True,
        use_cache=False,
    )

    quant_config = {
        "zero_point":   zero_point,
        "q_group_size": q_group_size,
        "w_bit":        w_bit,
        "version":      "GEMM",    # GEMM or GEMV kernel
    }

    print("  Running AWQ scale search...")
    model.quantize(
        tokenizer,
        quant_config    = quant_config,
        calib_data      = "pileval",  # Calibration dataset
        n_samples       = 128,
        seqlen          = 512,
    )

    print(f"  Saving to {output_dir}...")
    model.save_quantized(output_dir, safetensors=True)
    tokenizer.save_pretrained(output_dir)

    print(f"  ✅ AWQ quantization complete!")
    return output_dir

if __name__ == "__main__":
    visualize_awq_insight()
```

```python name=quantization/method4_gguf.py
"""
METHOD 4: GGUF Quantization for llama.cpp
Runs on CPU, Mac, consumer hardware. No GPU needed.
"""
import os, subprocess
from pathlib import Path

def explain_gguf_formats():
    """Explain all GGUF quantization formats."""
    print("""
    GGUF QUANTIZATION FORMATS:
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

    FORMAT      BITS   SIZE(7B)   QUALITY    USE CASE
    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    Q2_K        2.63   2.67 GB    ████░     Tiny RAM, low quality
    Q3_K_S      3.0    3.16 GB    █████     Very small
    Q3_K_M      3.0    3.52 GB    █████     Small
    Q4_0        4.0    3.83 GB    ██████    Fast, basic
    Q4_K_S      4.0    4.14 GB    ███████   Better than Q4_0
    Q4_K_M      4.37   4.37 GB    ████████  ← RECOMMENDED DEFAULT
    Q5_0        5.0    4.77 GB    ████████  Higher quality
    Q5_K_M      5.0    4.78 GB    █████████ High quality
    Q6_K        6.0    5.53 GB    █████████ Near FP16 quality
    Q8_0        8.0    7.66 GB    ██████████ Best quality
    F16         16.0  14.00 GB    ██████████ No quantization

    K-QUANT EXPLANATION:
    ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    "K" = uses mixed precision within the model
    Different layer types get different quantization levels:

    Q4_K_M means:
    - Most FFN layers: 4-bit
    - Attention layers: 5-bit or 6-bit (more important!)
    - Embeddings: 8-bit
    - Average: ~4.5 bits

    This is smarter than uniform 4-bit everywhere!
    Same size, better quality → the "M" means "medium" balance.

    S = small (most aggressive quantization)
    M = medium (balanced)
    L = large (higher quality, same bit count)
    """)

def convert_to_gguf(
    hf_model_path: str,
    output_path:   str,
    quant_type:    str = "q4_k_m",
):
    """
    Convert HuggingFace model to GGUF and quantize.
    Requires llama.cpp installed.

    Steps:
    1. Convert HF model → GGUF (FP16)
    2. Quantize GGUF FP16 → target format

    Install llama.cpp:
    git clone https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp
    cd llama.cpp && make
    pip install -r requirements.txt
    """
    llama_cpp_dir = Path(os.getenv("LLAMA_CPP_DIR", "./llama.cpp"))

    output_path = Path(output_path)
    output_path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    fp16_path = output_path / "model-fp16.gguf"
    quant_path= output_path / f"model-{quant_type}.gguf"

    # Step 1: Convert to GGUF (FP16)
    print(f"  Converting {hf_model_path} to GGUF FP16...")
    cmd_convert = [
        "python",
        str(llama_cpp_dir / "convert_hf_to_gguf.py"),
        hf_model_path,
        "--outtype", "f16",
        "--outfile", str(fp16_path),
    ]

    result = subprocess.run(
        cmd_convert, capture_output=True, text=True
    )
    if result.returncode != 0:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Conversion failed: {result.stderr}"
        )
    print(f"  ✅ FP16 GGUF saved: {fp16_path}")

    # Step 2: Quantize to target format
    print(f"  Quantizing to {quant_type.upper()}...")
    cmd_quantize = [
        str(llama_cpp_dir / "llama-quantize"),
        str(fp16_path),
        str(quant_path),
        quant_type.upper(),
    ]

    result = subprocess.run(
        cmd_quantize, capture_output=True, text=True
    )
    if result.returncode != 0:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Quantization failed: {result.stderr}"
        )

    # Get file sizes
    fp16_size  = fp16_path.stat().st_size  / 1e9
    quant_size = quant_path.stat().st_size / 1e9
    ratio      = quant_size / fp16_size

    print(f"  ✅ Quantized GGUF saved: {quant_path}")
    print(f"  FP16: {fp16_size:.2f} GB → "
          f"{quant_type.upper()}: {quant_size:.2f} GB "
          f"({ratio:.0%} of FP16)")

    return str(quant_path)

def run_gguf_inference(
    model_path: str,
    prompt:     str,
    n_predict:  int = 200,
    n_gpu_layers:int= 0,   # 0=CPU only, -1=all on GPU
):
    """
    Run inference with GGUF model using llama-cpp-python.
    Works on CPU without any GPU!
    """
    from llama_cpp import Llama

    print(f"\n  Loading GGUF: {model_path}")
    print(f"  GPU layers: {n_gpu_layers} "
          f"({'CPU only' if n_gpu_layers==0 else 'GPU accelerated'})")

    llm = Llama(
        model_path   = model_path,
        n_ctx        = 4096,          # Context window
        n_gpu_layers = n_gpu_layers,  # How many layers on GPU
        n_threads    = 8,             # CPU threads
        verbose      = False,
    )

    output = llm(
        prompt,
        max_tokens  = n_predict,
        temperature = 0.7,
        stop        = ["\n\n", "Human:", "User:"],
        echo        = False,
    )

    response = output["choices"][0]["text"]
    print(f"  Response: {response[:200]}")

    # Performance stats
    if "usage" in output:
        usage = output["usage"]
        print(f"  Tokens: {usage.get('completion_tokens')} generated")

    return response

def download_prebuilt_gguf(
    repo_id:   str,
    filename:  str,
    save_dir:  str = "./models",
):
    """
    Download pre-quantized GGUF from HuggingFace.
    Easiest way to get started!

    Example repos:
    - "TheBloke/LLaMA-2-7B-GGUF"
    - "TheBloke/Mistral-7B-v0.1-GGUF"
    - "bartowski/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-GGUF"
    """
    from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

    print(f"  Downloading {filename} from {repo_id}...")
    path = hf_hub_download(
        repo_id   = repo_id,
        filename  = filename,
        local_dir = save_dir,
    )
    print(f"  ✅ Downloaded: {path}")
    return path

if __name__ == "__main__":
    explain_gguf_formats()

    # Download a pre-quantized model (easiest approach)
    # model_path = download_prebuilt_gguf(
    #     repo_id  = "bartowski/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-GGUF",
    #     filename = "Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf",
    # )

    # Run CPU inference
    # run_gguf_inference(
    #     model_path  = model_path,
    #     prompt      = "What is quantization in ML?",
    #     n_gpu_layers= 0,   # Pure CPU
    # )
```

```python name=quantization/comparison_demo.py
"""
COMPLETE QUANTIZATION COMPARISON
Side-by-side: memory, speed, quality across all methods.
"""
import torch, time, os
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class QuantResult:
    method:     str
    bits:       float
    model_size: float   # GB
    load_time:  float   # seconds
    tokens_per_sec: float
    quality_score:  float  # 0-100
    sample_output:  str

def print_comparison_table(results: list[QuantResult]):
    """Print formatted comparison of all quantization methods."""
    print(f"\n{'═'*75}")
    print(f"  QUANTIZATION COMPARISON: {results[0].method.split('_')[0] if results else ''}")
    print(f"{'═'*75}")
    print(f"  {'Method':20s} {'Bits':5s} {'Size':8s} "
          f"{'Tok/s':7s} {'Quality':8s} {'Memory Saved'}")
    print(f"  {'─'*70}")

    baseline_size = max(r.model_size for r in results)

    for r in results:
        saved = (1 - r.model_size / baseline_size) * 100
        bar   = "█" * int(r.quality_score / 10)
        print(f"  {r.method:20s} {r.bits:5.1f} {r.model_size:6.1f}GB "
              f"{r.tokens_per_sec:6.0f}/s {bar:10s} "
              f"{r.quality_score:4.0f}% "
              f"saved {saved:4.0f}%")

    print(f"  {'─'*70}")

def quantization_decision_guide():
    """Print a decision guide for choosing quantization method."""
    print("""
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           QUANTIZATION DECISION GUIDE                           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Q: What hardware do I have?
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Mac (Apple Silicon M1/M2/M3/M4)
  → Use: MLX quantization or GGUF (Metal acceleration)
  → Command: mlx_lm.convert --hf-path model --mlx-path out -q

  NVIDIA GPU (8GB-24GB VRAM)
  → Use: GPTQ 4-bit or AWQ 4-bit
  → Best: AWQ for quality, GPTQ for compatibility

  CPU only (no GPU / running on server)
  → Use: GGUF Q4_K_M (llama.cpp)
  → Runs on: any CPU, even Raspberry Pi (slowly)!

  Q: What am I trying to do?
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Fine-tuning (QLoRA):
  → Use: BitsAndBytes NF4
  → Why: Compatible with PEFT LoRA training
  → Config: load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4"

  Production inference (GPU):
  → Use: AWQ 4-bit
  → Why: Best quality/speed balance, fast GEMM kernels
  → Or: vLLM with AWQ/GPTQ for batched serving

  Local development / testing:
  → Use: GGUF Q4_K_M
  → Why: Easy download, CPU-compatible, no setup

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```
